sets.quasar: A quasar in the early universe. Deep-navy bg with a small reddish young galaxy of faint stars; in the centre a black hole as a pure black disc with a thin cream photon ring, wrapped in a huge flat tilted accretion disc of white-hot inner rings fading to orange and red outer rings, 4 px outlines on the disc edges; setp.t 0..1 = disc rotation and camera drift; setp.jets 0..1 = two thin cyan-white jets shoot up and down out of the poles; setp.feed 0..1 = streams of gas spiral in from the galaxy into the disc; setp.outshine 0..1 = a white glare blooms until the galaxy's stars fade under it; setp.close 0..1 = camera pushes right up to the photon ring; setp.glow 'gold'|'cyan'|'red'.
sets.beam: Riding a beam of light. Deep-navy bg of deep space with stars streaking past in parallax; a long glowing cream-white light ribbon runs left to right across the frame like a road with a wave pattern along it, Pip rides on top of it; setp.t 0..1 = speed of the streaks; setp.stretch 0..1 = the wave pattern on the ribbon stretches longer and the ribbon colour shifts from blue-white (0) to orange (0.5) to deep red (1); setp.grid 0..1 = a faint cream square grid behind everything stretches wider (space expanding); setp.glow 'gold'|'cyan'|'red'.
sets.dawn: The cosmic dawn. Dark navy-black bg filled with thick dark grey-violet hydrogen fog; the first stars pop on as big blue-white points with soft blooms, and around them round bubbles of clear space grow and merge; small reddish baby galaxies drift in the clear bubbles; setp.stars 0..1 = how many first stars are lit; setp.clear 0..1 = how much fog the bubbles have cleared (0 almost all fog, 1 clear space); setp.t 0..1 = slow drift; setp.glow 'gold'|'cyan'.
sets.timeline: A cosmic timeline. Deep-navy bg; one long glowing gold line from a white BIG BANG burst on the far left to a small blue Earth labelled NOW on the far right, with outlined milestone dots and cream calendar-style tags (QUASAR 630 MYR, MILKY WAY, SUN 4.6 BYR, NOW); setp.now 0..1 = a bright cyan light spark (the photon) glides along the line from left to right; setp.t 0..1 = the camera pans along the line; setp.mark 0..4 = milestone tags pop up one by one; setp.glow 'gold'|'cyan'.
sets.euclid: ESA's Euclid telescope in deep space. Deep-navy bg with a faint band of distant galaxies; the Euclid spacecraft big in frame: white-silver tube body with dark aperture, a large flat dark-blue solar-panel sunshield, gold service module, 4 px outlines; a thin cyan field-of-view cone reaches out of the aperture; setp.t 0..1 = slow orbit drift; setp.scan 0..1 = the cone sweeps across the galaxy band leaving cream square survey tiles behind; setp.catch 0..1 = a single small red spark arrives from the left and enters the aperture with a bright flash at 1; setp.glow 'gold'|'cyan'.
sets.field: A deep sky survey image. Black bg crowded with hundreds of tiny galaxies (cream, lilac, orange ellipses and spirals) and white stars with small spikes; one tiny red dot near the centre; setp.zoom 0..1 = camera pushes from the whole crowded field down to the red dot; setp.mark 0..1 = a cream circle draws on around the red dot with a short cream leader line; setp.count 0..1 = more and more objects fade in (millions); setp.glow 'gold'|'cyan'|'red'.
sets.spectrum: Redshift explained. Deep-navy bg; a wide outlined rainbow strip across the frame from violet on the left through blue, green, yellow, orange, red, then a dark maroon zone labelled INFRARED on the far right; a glowing marker spark sits above it; setp.z 0..1 = the marker slides from blue (0) through red to deep in the infrared (1); setp.wave 0..1 = a thick wave line under the strip stretches to match; setp.eye 0..1 = a big simple outlined human eye icon over the visible part fades to a closed eye when the marker passes red; setp.glow 'gold'|'cyan'|'red'.
sets.earthnight: Earth at night. A dark blue sky full of stars over a soft grassy hill silhouette with a few warm house lights far away; Pip stands on the hill; setp.t 0..1 = slow star drift; setp.dot 0..1 = one faint red point high in the sky brightens a little and gets a cream ring; setp.milky 0..1 = a soft Milky Way band fades in across the sky; setp.glow 'gold'|'cyan'.
sets.growth: Black hole growth chart. Deep-navy bg; on the left a tiny black-hole seed (black dot with thin ring), on the right a huge black hole with a fiery orange disc; between them a steep outlined gold curve on simple axes (TIME across, MASS up) with a short cream bracket labelled FIRST 630 MILLION YEARS; setp.grow 0..1 = the curve draws on and the black hole on the right swells; setp.t 0..1 = slow push; setp.burst 0..1 = three bright jagged steps appear on the curve (rapid growth spurts); setp.glow 'gold'|'red'|'cyan'.
sets.fort: Dún Aonghasa, a prehistoric stone fort on a cliff edge on Inis Mór, Ireland, at dusk: curved dry-stone walls in grey on green grass at the top of a sheer cliff with the Atlantic Ocean below and a huge starry sky above; one small red star glows over the horizon; setp.t 0..1 = slow pan out toward the sea; setp.stars 0..1 = the stars come out; setp.glow 'gold'|'cyan'.
sets.void: Plain deep-navy SpaceBackdrop stage with slow light rays and almost no stars, for big numbers, bars and diagrams. setp.glow 'gold'|'cyan'|'red' tints the rays.

props.counter: Big flat panel, 4 px dark outline, dark #1E1B2E face, cream flip digits in FONTS.title with thousands separators, label in FONTS.ui underneath. pp.from and pp.to: the number counts from->to across the shot (ease-out); pp.label text; pp.color gold|red|cyan.
props.clock: Round analogue clock face, cream disc, 4 px dark outline, ticks, one hand. pp.from..pp.to in hours: the hand sweeps; pp.glow true adds a gold bloom.
props.bar: Horizontal progress bar with 4 px outline, filled with pp.color (gold|red|cyan) to pp.frac of its width over the shot; pp.label above in FONTS.ui.
props.arrow: Thick outlined curved arrow, pp.color gold|cyan|red, draws on across the shot.
props.flag: Small green check mark badge in a round outlined cream disc with a tiny sparkle; or red cross when pp.bad true.
props.calendar: Small wall calendar page, cream with a red top strip, 4 px outline; pp.text the date in FONTS.title (max 8 chars).
props.magnifier: Outlined magnifying glass with a cream handle and pale glass; pp.s scale; pp.glow true adds a cyan bloom in the lens.
props.ring: Pulsing cyan circle outline, 4 px, soft bloom, that expands and fades each second; pp.s scale.
props.scale: Small balance scale icon, cream, 4 px outline, one pan tipped low; pp.s scale; pp.label text beneath.
props._probe_old: Icon of the BepiColombo stack: a small gold-foil box body with two dark solar-panel wings, a round grey antenna dish and a silver conical sunshield on top, 4 px outline; pp.s scale; pp.glow true adds an orange thruster flame at the bottom.
props.thermo: Tall outlined thermometer, cream glass tube, red or blue fluid to pp.frac (0..1), pp.label text beneath in FONTS.ui; pp.color red|cyan.
props.euclid: Icon of ESA's Euclid space telescope: a white-silver tube body with a dark open aperture, a big flat dark-blue solar-panel sunshield on one side and a small gold service module below, 4 px outline; pp.s scale; pp.glow true adds a soft cyan bloom at the aperture.
props.webb: Icon of the James Webb Space Telescope: a gold hexagon-segment mirror on a dark boom with a silver diamond sunshield below, 4 px outline; pp.s scale; pp.glow true adds a soft gold bloom.
props.bh: Small black-hole icon: a pure black disc with a thin bright cream photon ring and a tilted orange-gold accretion disc around it, 4 px outline; pp.s scale; pp.glow true adds a hot white-gold bloom; pp.jets true adds two thin cyan jets up and down.
props.sun: Small outlined yellow Sun disc with short rays and a tiny smile-free face-less glow, 4 px outline; pp.s scale; pp.label optional text beneath in FONTS.ui.
props.galaxy: Small outlined spiral galaxy icon, cream core and two lilac arms, 4 px outline on the core; pp.s scale; pp.red true tints it reddish (young, far galaxy).
props.wave: A horizontal light wave squiggle, thick outlined line; pp.stretch 0..1: across the shot the wiggles get longer and fewer while the colour slides from blue (0) to red (0.6) to dark infrared maroon (1); pp.label optional text above in FONTS.ui.
props.photon: A tiny glowing cream-white light spark with a short comet-like streak behind it, 4 px outline on the core; pp.s scale; pp.color white|red sets the core tint.
props.plate: An outlined cream dinner plate seen at a slight angle with a fork beside it and one tiny glowing crumb in the middle; pp.s scale.
props.tag: Outlined cream tag on a short string with pp.text in FONTS.ui (max 12 chars); pp.color gold|cyan|red sets the string and underline.
props.earth: Small outlined blue-green Earth ball with white cloud swirls, 4 px outline; pp.s scale; pp.young true makes it a glowing orange molten ball instead.

actions.lookup: Pip tilts head back, arms loose, small sway; eyes lift at p 0.2.
actions.duck: Pip drops into a crouch with both arms over the head at p 0.15 and holds with a small tremble.
actions.spin: Pip turns one slow full rotation across the shot while looking around.
actions.flinch: A quick squash and lean away at p 0.2 with arms up, then settles back by p 0.7.
actions.pointup: Pip's arm swings up to point up at p 0.2 with a small overshoot.

film.vo: You have been flying for thirteen billion years.
And you are about to hit a telescope.
You are a single speck of light.
From the most distant quasar ever found.
When you left home, the universe was a baby.
Earth did not exist. The Sun did not exist. Nothing you know existed.
And what made you? A black hole.
film.dir: awed, slow; stress 'three hundred sixty million'

film.vo: Three hundred sixty million times heavier than the Sun.
film.dir: awed, slow; stress 'three hundred sixty million'

film.vo: ESA's Euclid telescope just announced it. A brand new record.
So what if you were that light.
And you rode the whole way here?
First, the rules. You are one photon. One tiny packet of light.
You move at about three hundred thousand kilometres every second.
Earth to the Moon? About one and a bit seconds.
Rule two: you cannot stop. You cannot slow down. You cannot turn.
No snack breaks. No toilet. Thirteen billion years in a straight line.
Rule three is the strange one. Space itself will stretch you.
Remember that. It is the reason anyone can find you at all.
Now, where does your trip begin?
You start your life six hundred thirty million years after the Big Bang.
film.dir: grand, steady; stress 'six hundred thirty million'

film.vo: That sounds old. For the universe, it is barely out of nappies.
It is only about five percent of its age today.
You are born in the heart of a young, reddish galaxy.
And at that heart sits something enormous.
A supermassive black hole.
Gas spirals in around it like water down a plughole.
The gas rubs, heats up, and glows brighter than anything around it.
That blazing core is called a quasar.
A quasar can outshine every star in its own galaxy put together.
Imagine a torch so bright it hides the whole city behind it.
Webb later weighed this black hole: about three hundred sixty million Suns.
Line up our Sun three hundred sixty million times.
That is one black hole.
You are flung out of that glare in a fraction of a second.
Bad news: you are not the only light leaving. Trillions leave with you.
Almost all of them will never hit anything we can see. You will.
But first, the universe you are flying through looks nothing like ours.
It is foggy out here. Thick clouds of hydrogen gas everywhere.
For a long time after the Big Bang, the universe was dark.
Now the very first stars and galaxies are switching on.
Each new star blows a bubble of clear space around itself.
The bubbles grow and join, like lights coming on across a city.
ESA calls it the moment a dark universe filled with light.
You are flying right through it. Front row seats.
You pass baby galaxies. Small, messy, red, and full of new stars.
Some of them will one day grow into giants like our Milky Way.
Our own galaxy? Not finished. Not even close.
And that quasar behind you? It is a puzzle nobody can explain yet.
Hold that thought. We will come back to it.
Because something is happening to you. You are changing colour.
Here is rule three in action. The universe is expanding.
Every bit of space between the galaxies keeps getting bigger.
And as space stretches, it stretches you with it.
Light is a wave. Short waves look blue. Long waves look red.
Your waves are being pulled longer and longer.
Astronomers call this redshift. Yours is eight point one three.
That number is a record. No quasar had ever been found beyond eight.
In plain words.
Your waves end up about nine times longer than when you left.
You were blazing ultraviolet and blue. Now you are deep red.
Then past red. Into infrared, a colour human eyes cannot see.
Congratulations. You are now invisible. Also very, very long.
Remember why the stretch matters? To find you, a telescope needs infrared eyes.
That telescope will not even exist for thirteen billion years.
So you settle in. This is going to take a while.
One billion years go by. Then two. Then five.
Galaxies crash together. Spirals form. Our Milky Way slowly takes shape.
You are still flying. Still red. Still going.
Around nine billion years into your trip.
A cloud collapses in a quiet corner of the Milky Way.
It becomes our Sun, about four point six billion years ago.
Think about that. You are older than the Sun. By billions of years.
film.dir: awed, slower; stress 'older than the Sun'

film.vo: Then a hot little ball forms near the new Sun. Earth.
It cools down, grows oceans, and, very slowly, grows life.
Dinosaurs come and go. You do not care. You are a photon.
film.dir: comic deadpan; stress 'you do not care'

film.vo: Humans show up. They build fires, then cities, then telescopes.
All of human history fits into the last blink of your trip.
And here is the wild part.
Space has kept stretching behind you the whole time.
So home is now far, far more than thirteen billion light-years away.
You could never fly back. Not that you were allowed to turn.
Then, in your last few years, something new appears up ahead.
In twenty twenty-three, Europe launches the Euclid space telescope.
Its job: map the dark universe across a huge patch of sky.
And it has exactly what you need: very sensitive infrared eyes.
Your thirteen billion year trip ends on its detector.
Splat. Well, a tiny electric blip. But still, you made it.
In the picture, you are not a blazing beacon.
You are a red dot.
And you are one dot among millions of objects.
Scientists sifted through about eighteen months of Euclid data to spot you.
Finding you was harder than finding one grain of sand on a beach.
But a red dot could be a lot of things.
A nearby cool star. A dusty galaxy.
So the big telescopes were called in.
Keck in Hawaii. The Large Binocular Telescope.
Then Hubble. And finally, Webb.
Webb split your light and confirmed it. You really are a quasar.
Its nickname is Dún Aonghasa.
Its official name is J fifteen-oh-four plus sixty-two fifty-two.
It is named after an ancient stone fort.
On a cliff edge in Ireland.
Like that fort.
This quasar sits right at the edge of what we can see.
Now, remember the puzzle? Here it is.
Black holes grow by eating gas.
Big ones need a lot of time to get big.
This one had only six hundred thirty million years since the Big Bang.
And it still reached three hundred sixty million Suns.
Here is the twist. Right now, this quasar is a slow eater.
ESA says it is eating at a relatively slow rate.
So how did a slow eater get that huge, that fast?
It is like meeting a toddler the size of a house.
film.dir: comic image; stress 'size of a house'

film.vo: Who barely eats.
film.dir: comic image; stress 'size of a house'

film.vo: The answer, scientists think, is short, wild growth spurts very early on.
Feasting so hard, so fast, that our models struggle to keep up.
That is why this little red dot matters so much.
It is a clue to how the first giant black holes were born.
And it is not the only red dot Euclid has caught.
film.dir: teasing, leading on; stress 'not the only'

film.vo: This find beats Euclid's own record, set just a few months earlier.
It looks back an extra forty million years.
In just a year and a half.
Euclid has announced thirty-one ancient quasars.
Twelve of them sit beyond redshift seven.
Older surveys took fifteen years just to reach that distance.
Euclid more than doubled the known count out there.
But at redshift eight.

text.text: AT Z 8: A FEW TENS, MAX

film.vo: They are so rare that ESA expects a few tens at most.
In the whole survey. That is how special your little trip was.
So somewhere out there, older light is still on its way.
film.dir: wonder, rising; stress 'still on its way'

film.vo: Every new record pushes the edge a little further back.
film.dir: building to the end; stress 'further back'

film.vo: So back to that moment. Thirteen billion years, and you hit a telescope.
You left before the Sun. Before Earth. Before anyone could look up.
And someone finally did look up, just in time to catch you.
film.dir: warm, landing it; stress 'just in time'

film.vo: Every time you look at the night sky.
film.dir: the takeaway, gentle; stress 'back in time'

film.vo: You are looking back in time.
film.dir: the takeaway, gentle; stress 'back in time'

film.vo: Which would you rather ride: the oldest light, or the brightest?
Tell me in the comments.
Tomorrow: what if you rode a nuclear-powered spaceship to Mars?

short.vo: This red dot is a giant black hole.
Its light left thirteen billion years ago, before the Sun existed.
ESA's Euclid telescope spotted it. A new record.
Gas falls into the black hole and outshines its whole galaxy.
We see it six hundred thirty million years after the Big Bang.
Space stretched its light nine times, into invisible infrared.
So it shows up red, and only infrared eyes can spot it.
Webb weighed it: three hundred sixty million Suns.
The twist? We catch it eating slowly.
So how did it get that huge, that fast? Nobody knows yet.
Best guess: wild growth spurts, very early on.
So every time you look up, you are looking back in time.
Full film on the channel. And this red dot? A giant black hole.
short.dir: friendly, looping to the start; stress 'red dot'
